newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila oil firms say price hike not inflationary.
newsitem.headline: Manila oil firms say price hike not inflationary.

text.p: Philippine oil refiners said on Friday the new round of increases in local petroleum prices should not fuel inflation since oil prices were higher before the industry was deregulated in February.
The oil firms raised their prices because they have to pay for more dollars for their crude imports since the de facto devaluation of the peso in July.
"The effect should be minimal, consumption-wise and inflation-wise," Frank Cruz, vice-president for logistics at Caltex (Philippines) Inc told Reuters.
The oil price hike, though, may indeed be a "perfect excuse" for companies to take advantage of the peso's weakness and begin adjusting prices, Cruz said.

"We believe there is no reason for commodity prices to go up as a result of these price adjustments. We have been at a higher price level before February and at that time, inflation was at a very low rate," Pilipinas Shell Petroleum Corp general manager Reynaldo Gamboa said earlier.

The new average wholesale posted price of petroleum products at 6.71 pesos a litre was still 24 centavos cheaper than the average price of 6.95 pesos before the industry was fully deregulated in February, Gamboa said.

Pilipinas Shell Petroleum Corp late on Thursday said it was raising petroleum prices by an average of 23 centavos per litre effective August 1. It was the first to announce an oil price hike after the peso was effectively devalued three weeks ago.
Petron Corp, which is 40 percent-owned by the Philippine government, followed and said it would also raise the prices of all its petroleum products.
Caltex (Philippines) Inc raised its prices similar to Petron's.
The price adjustments did not include foreign exchange losses from dollar- denominated loans.
Cause-oriented groups have been opposing an oil price hike since it will trigger increases in the prices of other basic goods.

Raul Concepcion, president of the Federation of Philippine Industries told Reuters the oil price hikes will have little effect on basic goods since oil firms tempered the increase on "socially sensitive products" such as diesel, liquefied petroleum gasoline and fuel oil.
The bulk of the increases were absorbed by gasoline products.
"They were supposed to increase prices by 80 centavos but they did not pass on the entire amount. There should be no effect on prices of basic commodities," said Concepcion.

Concepcion also said the oil price increases would not have an immediate impact on power rates since the National Power Corp (Napocor) promised to ward off any increase in power rates until this month.
Napocor, which largely depends on fuel oil and diesel, had said it had enough dollars and inventory of fuel to postpone a power rate increase until this month.
Despite the effect of a tumbling peso, fierce competition in the industry brought on by deregulation will stave off sharp increases in oil prices, oil company officials said.
"We just aligned our prices with the new entrants. Competition will continue at the same intensity. It is keeping a rein on prices," Cruz said.
Shell's Gamboa said the refiner will maintain and even improve on its existing 37 percent market share.
"We aim to be the leading marketer," Gamboa said.
